title: Applying Multiple Utilities
subtopics: Grouping layout, spacing, typography, and state classes
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of applying multiple utilities.
Apply one appropriate technique to a small Tailwind CSS example.
Verify the expected result and identify a common failure mode.

content.intro: In this lesson, focus on applying multiple utilities and connect it to the way Tailwind CSS generates and applies utility styles.
content.why_it_matters: The reliability of applying multiple utilities affects whether Tailwind detects candidate classes and generates the CSS you expect at build time.

content_blocks.title: Module 4 learning map
content_blocks.alt_text: Four-step module learning map: Understanding Utility-Class Naming → Understanding Variants → Handling Dynamic Class Names Correctly → Establishing a Reliable Utility-Class Workflow. Lesson pages add code examples and practice.
content_blocks.caption: Learning map for Module 4, from the opening concept to a practical checkpoint.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum highlights: Combining independent utilities; Organizing class attributes; Grouping layout, spacing, typography, and state classes; Reading long utility strings; Avoiding conflicting classes. Treat these as practical decisions rather than a list to memorize: identify the intended behavior, choose the smallest suitable utility or directive, and inspect what the browser receives.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the example, change one decision related to applying multiple utilities, then compare the outcome. In a Tailwind-enabled project, confirm the generated CSS exists; class strings alone do not make styles available without a configured build.

content_blocks.title: Version and compatibility note
content_blocks.text: This course prioritizes Tailwind CSS v4. Confirm your installed version and use its matching official guide. Snippets using v3 directives or configuration are labelled as legacy and should not be mixed blindly with v4 syntax.

content.task: Create a minimal example demonstrating applying multiple utilities. Include a before/after comparison and explain why the chosen utility, variant or directive is appropriate.
task_acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate at least one decision tied to applying multiple utilities.
Keep the example easy to inspect, with complete utility names.
Test the outcome and document one limitation or environment assumption.
hints: Identify which listed syllabus topic is most important to applying multiple utilities.
Change one utility, token, variant or configuration setting at a time.
Inspect generated CSS and computed styles before changing unrelated code.
content.expected_output: A centered content section with a prominent heading and readable paragraph; rendering requires the configured Tailwind build.
troubleshooting: If no style appears, verify the package, CSS import and build-tool integration before changing the HTML.
If only a state or breakpoint style fails, check the full class token, source detection, condition and computed CSS.
For a framework snippet, import the stylesheet through its supported entry point and consult the current official guide.
common_mistakes: Applying applying multiple utilities without checking generated styles or browser behavior.
Mixing Tailwind v3 and v4 setup examples without a migration plan.
Treating visual appearance as a substitute for semantic markup, keyboard usability or actual component behavior.
summary: Applying Multiple Utilities is one part of a predictable utility-first styling workflow.
Keep examples small, test the built interface and use version-matched documentation.
